summary: Changes the PIM Sparse Mode Join message format so a node can attach extra attributes when it joins a multicast tree. Before this there was no way to pass such additional information. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 7887.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5384 adds a format for attaching extra attributes to a PIM Sparse Mode Join. It defines how routers carry and process the attributes, while leaving each attribute's meaning to a separate specification.

subtitle: A way for PIM routers to attach typed attributes to a multicast-tree Join.

tldr.problem: A PIM Sparse Mode Join identifies a group and source, but did not provide a standard place for extra information about how to build that multicast tree.
tldr.mechanism: A new Encoded-Source Address encoding type, type 1, carries Join Attributes as Type-Length-Value fields. A PIM Hello option lets a router indicate that it can receive this encoding.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the container and general processing rules, not any particular attribute. It is updated by RFC 7887.

today: RFC 5384 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7887. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why PIM Joins Need Attributes
sections.content:
A PIM Sparse Mode Join identifies a multicast distribution tree using a multicast group address and a source address, which may be a wildcard. Some applications need to provide extra information about building that tree. This RFC adds a way to associate such information with the tree.

It defines Encoded-Source Address type 1. The address retains the normal source information and can also carry Join Attributes encoded as Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields. Type 0 remains the native source encoding. This RFC defines no specific Join Attribute and does not cover PIM Dense Mode.
sections.plainLanguage: A PIM Join can now carry extra information about the tree it requests. This RFC defines the carrying format, not the meaning of any one attribute.

sections.title: The Type 1 Attribute Encoding
sections.content:
Type 1 Encoded-Source Addresses contain at least one Join Attribute. If a tree has no attributes, the sender uses type 0. Multiple attributes of the same or different types may appear, and there is no separate count field; the last attribute is marked in its header.

Each attribute has an F bit, an E bit, a 6-bit Attr_Type, a one-octet Length and the value. F marks a transitive attribute; E marks the final attribute in the sequence. Length gives the value size in octets. The source address is encoded the same way as in type 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute says what type it is, how long its value is, and whether it must be forwarded. A final-attribute bit tells a router where the list ends.

sections.title: Advertising Support with a PIM Hello
sections.content:
A router that cannot parse type 1 cannot process a Join that contains it. The RFC therefore defines the Join Attribute option for PIM Hello messages. A router willing to receive type 1 MUST include the option in its Hellos.

A router MUST NOT send a type 1 address through an interface if any PIM neighbor on that interface has not advertised the option. The option only indicates support for the encoding. It does not guarantee that the router understands every attribute type.
sections.plainLanguage: A router must advertise that it can parse attribute-bearing Joins before a neighbor sends them. That announcement does not mean it understands every attribute's meaning.

sections.title: Processing Unknown and Conflicting Attributes
sections.content:
A router must examine attributes in their listed order. Each attribute specification defines what to do with repeated instances. If a router does not understand an attribute, the F bit decides whether it forwards or discards it: a set bit requires forwarding; a clear bit requires discarding. If no attributes remain, the router forwards a type 0 Join.

Attributes of the same type can conflict when they arrive from different downstream neighbors. Unless that attribute has its own conflict rule, the router selects the value from the adjacency with the numerically smallest IP address; the interface index breaks a tie. A router may remember alternatives to switch quickly if the selected neighbor withdraws.
sections.plainLanguage: A router forwards an unknown attribute only when its F bit says to do so. When neighbors provide conflicting values, the default rule selects the one from the lowest-address adjacency.

sections.title: Replacing an Attribute Set
sections.content:
A new Join replaces the entire prior attribute set for that tree. There are no incremental updates: an attribute missing from the new Join is withdrawn. If a router changes attributes but keeps the same upstream neighbor, it must send a new Join containing the new set. An empty set uses type 0.

If the upstream neighbor changes, the router sends a Prune to the old neighbor; the Prune does not need attributes. A downstream Prune withdraws the attributes that neighbor previously supplied, and the router may then need to update its own upstream Join.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new Join gives the complete current attribute set. Any old attribute left out of that Join is withdrawn.

sections.title: Registries and Assigned Values
sections.content:
IANA created the PIM Join Attribute Types registry for the Attr_Type field. Allocations use IETF Review. IANA also assigned PIM Hello option value 26 to the Join Attribute option.

The RFC establishes a registry for Encoded-Source Address encoding types. Type 0 is the native address-family encoding defined by RFC 4601; type 1 is the native encoding with PIM Join Attributes defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the official lists of attribute types and encoding types. The Join Attribute Hello option has value 26.

sections.title: Deployment and Security
sections.content:
Join Attributes receive only the security protection provided to the PIM packet that carries them. A particular attribute may need additional security rules, which its own specification must describe. The security considerations for Bidirectional PIM may also apply.

A router that does not understand type 1 cannot process that Join. If an attribute affects tree construction, every router that receives it must understand both the encoding and that attribute for the tree to be built correctly. The RFC therefore limits useful deployment to one administrative domain or a small group of cooperating domains where support is known in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes are only dependable when the routers along the path can process them. Their security depends on PIM and on any extra rules defined for the attribute.
